sections.title: Upgrades and backups
sections.html:
How to update Orbit, how to back it up, and how to go back if an update goes wrong. Run every command on this page from the deployment directory, the one you installed into.

The short version: back up, check the backup, update, and check that Orbit is healthy and you can sign in. Keep the backup until you are sure.

sections.title: Back up
sections.html:
#Back up

bash scripts/backup.sh

This makes one file in backups/, named like orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar, and prints Orbit backup created: followed by its path. The file holds a copy of the database and an encrypted copy of the stored documents.

  • Orbit is stopped while the backup runs, so the copy is of one moment in time, and is started again afterwards.
  • To keep backups somewhere else, set ORBIT_BACKUP_DIR to that directory when you run the script. If you set it, set it the same way for every backup, restore, --recover and --finish: a restore keeps its recovery record in that directory.
  • The host needs Docker with Compose v2. Orbit's document key file, .orbit-secrets/document-kek, must be in place.
  • A backup does not hold your settings (.env-orbit) or your secrets.

Check a backup at any time with:

bash scripts/backup.sh --verify backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar

This reads the file and changes nothing, and Orbit keeps running.

#A backup needs the document key

A backup is tied to the document encryption key it was made with, so it is only useful on a machine that still has that key. To be able to recover after losing the machine, also export a recovery bundle, protected by a passphrase, and keep it somewhere else. See Exporting a recovery bundle.

Backups, restores and updates are refused while a document key rotation is open. See Rotating the document key-encryption key.

sections.title: Update
sections.html:
#Update

  1. Back up, and check the backup, as above.
  2. Keep a copy of your settings next to it, in the same directory as the backup (backups, or your ORBIT_BACKUP_DIR). The copy records exactly which build was running, so you can go back to it:
    umask 077
mkdir -p backups
cp .env-orbit backups/orbit-pre-upgrade.env
  3. Run the install line from Installing Orbit again, in the deployment directory, and choose Update.

If it stops part-way, run the update again; see If an update stops.

Afterwards, open Orbit, check /api/health, and sign in. Keep using docker compose --env-file .env-orbit from the deployment directory, with no --project-name, so every command finds the same containers and data.

#Update from no more than three releases back

An install can update directly only from the last three stable releases before the one you are installing; retracted releases do not count. From further back, the installer stops before it pulls or changes anything and names the release to update to first, for example This install is on v0.3.1. Update to v0.3.4 first, then to v0.3.6.

To step through, install the release it names (pin it with its version tag, for example ORBIT_VERSION=v0.3.4, as in Installing Orbit), check /api/health, then run the update again for the next release. Each stop repeats the check, so a long way back takes a few steps. An install whose .env-orbit records an applied digest (ORBIT_CONFIG_APPLIED_DIGEST) but no ORBIT_CONFIG_APPLIED_VERSION, or is on a version that is not a stable release, is refused with a line saying so (an env file with neither is a fresh install); run bash scripts/repair.sh --check first.

sections.title: Go back after a failed update
sections.html:
#Go back after a failed update

If Orbit has started on the new build but the database update or sign-in then fails, stop it and restore both the backup and the saved settings:

docker compose --env-file .env-orbit stop orbit-app
cp backups/orbit-pre-upgrade.env .env-orbit
chmod 600 .env-orbit
docker compose --env-file .env-orbit pull orbit-app
bash scripts/restore.sh backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar

Use the backup you made in step 1 of the update. The saved .env-orbit names the previous build exactly, so do not swap in a version name or edit only ORBIT_IMAGE. Type RESTORE when it asks. Then check /api/health, check that you can sign in on the previous build, and only then delete the saved copy:

rm -f backups/orbit-pre-upgrade.env

Installer guarantees lists exactly what the installer promises around an upgrade.

sections.title: Restore
sections.html:
#Restore

bash scripts/restore.sh backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar

The restore checks the backup, stops Orbit, checks the backup again, and asks you to type RESTORE. If you do not, Orbit starts again unchanged. Once you do, it takes a recovery checkpoint, replaces the database and the stored documents with the ones in the backup, starts Orbit and waits for it to answer.

On a new machine, or any machine without the original document key, first put the key back from your recovery bundle: see Restoring the document key-encryption key. Then run the restore.

If a restore is interrupted part-way, or Orbit is not healthy afterwards, Orbit stays stopped and bash scripts/restore.sh --recover puts the previous state back. If Orbit is running the restored data but the restore says it could not finish, run bash scripts/restore.sh --finish. Until a restore is finished or recovered, new backups and restores are refused.

  • Both scripts run Orbit's engine inside the deployment, so the host needs Docker with Compose v2. Restore also needs curl, to wait for Orbit to answer; backup does not.

An unattended restore skips the typed RESTORE only when given both switches, so that neither alone can replace your data:

ORBIT_NONINTERACTIVE_RESTORE=true bash scripts/restore.sh --yes backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar

--yes without the variable stops before Orbit is touched.
